input:
It is worth noting that the lifetime values reported for the benchmark material differ quite substantially between the two groups, and this discrepancy arguably tells us more about the respective test conditions than about the material itself. The first group, for instance, measured lifetime on fresh beds under a dry feed and, perhaps unsurprisingly, reported the longer values, highlighting the stability of the material under favourable conditions. The second group, by contrast, worked with beds that had already been exposed to a humid feed, and its values are consistently lower right from the very first cycle onwards. When the two data sets are placed side by side, it becomes increasingly clear that they essentially describe two quite different ageing histories rather than two genuinely different materials, underscoring the importance of context when interpreting such results.

Another important factor in this comparison is the role of IAST. One group's lifetimes are based on breakthrough times predicted for mixtures, whereas the other group's lifetimes rest on direct mixture measurements, and this methodological difference should not be overlooked. Where the prediction and the measurement have actually been compared on the same bed, the prediction tends to run long, and the gap appears to widen as the feed humidity rises. This suggests that the dry-feed group's apparent advantage is, at least in part, an artefact of the route by which its numbers were obtained, with predicted lifetimes under relatively mild conditions being set against measured lifetimes obtained under noticeably harsher ones.

Overall, the measured values would seem to carry more weight, and a preference for the second group's figures as the basis for design therefore appears justified, albeit on one specific condition. That condition is that the design feed resembles the humid feed used in the measured tests. For a dry feed, the ranking is not really established by either data set, and the longer predicted lifetimes remain unconfirmed rather than wrong. What the comparison does ultimately settle is arguably narrower in scope: lifetime for the benchmark material is a function of feed humidity and ageing history, and a single lifetime value quoted without those conditions cannot simply be carried from one group's tests to the other's.

The lifetime values reported for the benchmark material differ between the two groups by more than either group's internal scatter, and the difference tracks the test conditions each group chose rather than any property of the material itself. One group measured lifetime on fresh beds under a dry feed and reported the longer values. The other group measured on beds that had already seen humid feed, and its values sit lower from the first cycle onward. Read side by side, the two data sets describe two different ageing histories more than they describe two different materials.

IAST enters the comparison because one group's lifetimes rest on breakthrough times predicted for mixtures, while the other group's rest on direct mixture measurements. Where the prediction and the measurement have been compared on the same bed, the prediction runs long, and the gap widens as the feed humidity rises. The dry-feed group's advantage is therefore partly an artefact of the route by which its numbers were obtained: predicted lifetimes under mild conditions stand against measured lifetimes under harsher ones.

On the evidence available, the measured values carry more weight, and the preference goes to the second group's figures as the basis for design, on one condition. The condition is that the design feed resembles the humid feed of the measured tests. For a dry feed the ranking is not established by either data set, and the longer predicted lifetimes remain unconfirmed rather than wrong. What the comparison settles is narrower: lifetime for the benchmark material is a function of feed humidity and ageing history, and a single lifetime quoted without those conditions cannot be carried from one group's tests to the other's. Neither group is contradicted on its own ground; the conflict appears only when a value measured or predicted under one set of conditions is read as a property of the material, detached from the conditions that produced it.
